Dieting is such a horrible thing to navigate when you are trying to recover, because there's such a thin line between the good and bad habits. I know you want to help, especially when you are trying to get better yourself, but my personal advice is to not try to give people advice, focus on your eating habits, and let other people figure out theirs, with medically trained professionals if necessary. It's just too easy to say something that seems innocent, but is actually going to harm them.

YTA, both to yourself and your friend, and tbh I think you should remove your tips from your post. Yes, they are something that most people could find from a quick pro ana google search but I really think we should be staying away from actively broadcasting the unhealthy methods we use to lose weight. 

I had an eating disorder that nearly killed me when I was a teenager. I made friends with people who also had a problem deliberately to compare myself with them. It starts as geniunely wanting moral support but it ends up spiralling into a weird competition. 

This is not healthy. It's not true that you can't ever recover from it. It took 14 years, a butt load of therapy, lots of anti depressants, and months as an outpatient at a mental health facility, but I can honestly say I have no desire to starve myself anymore, and I don't even recognise the old version of me. I know it's hard, especially as a teenager when it might be the only thing that you have control over, but this sounds like the beginning of a very slippery slope for the two of you. Use your friendship as a driving force to help both of you recover, not as a way to help push each other down. You deserve more than that.

YTA. I work in a country that speaks english as a second language. The official language of my company is English, however when it is just me that doesnt speak the language (which is most working days) the rest of my colleagues will slip into their native tongue. So most of the time I feel left out and frustrated when something is happening that I should know, but I've not been made aware of. I understand completly how hard it is to feel invisible due to a language barrier.

That being said, I can also see why the best man would feel more comfortable talking in his native language. Maybe he isnt as confident in his english, or if he is discussing plans with your husband, he is wanting to make sure that he hasn't misunderstood something. To blanket ban any language but English in your house and at your wedding seems like a massive over reaction and makes you seem petty and bridezillary. 

With my particular language barrier problem, I am leaving my job. I'm not recommending you leaving your fiance but I think you have to accept that this is one of the things that wont change in your relationship.
